## Question and data

I explore the relationship between flipper length and body mass,
using species colours to distinguish groups.

Data come from [Palmer Penguins](https://allisonhorst.github.io/palmerpenguins/),
collected by Kristen Gorman and Palmer Station Antarctica LTER.
The data have a CC0 licence and are included in the Python package.

Dataset package reference: Horst, A. M., Hill, A. P., and Gorman, K. B.
(2020). *palmerpenguins: Palmer Archipelago (Antarctica) penguin data.*
[doi:10.5281/zenodo.3960218](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.3960218).

## Setup

The setup chunk hides routine imports to keep attention on the analysis.
Analysis code and results remain visible.

```{python}
#| label: setup
#| echo: false
import sys
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from palmerpenguins import load_penguins
```

Confirm which Python executable is running this document.

```{python}
#| label: check-environment
print(sys.executable)
```

## Load and inspect

Check the dataset size and missing values in the variables used.

```{python}
#| label: inspect-data
penguins = load_penguins()
print("Original rows:", len(penguins))
print(penguins[["species", "flipper_length_mm", "body_mass_g"]].isna().sum())
penguins.head()
```

## Prepare the data

Remove rows missing a variable needed for the analysis.
Keep the original dataset unchanged.

```{python}
#| label: clean-data
clean = penguins.dropna(
    subset=["species", "flipper_length_mm", "body_mass_g"]
).copy()
print("Rows retained:", len(clean))
print("Rows excluded:", len(penguins) - len(clean))
```

## Summarize the relationship

Pearson correlation describes the direction and strength of a linear
relationship. Compare the pooled correlation with correlations within
each species, because species differences may affect the pooled result.

```{python}
#| label: summarize-relationship
overall_correlation = clean["flipper_length_mm"].corr(clean["body_mass_g"])
print(f"Overall Pearson correlation: {overall_correlation:.3f}")

for species, group in clean.groupby("species"):
    correlation = group["flipper_length_mm"].corr(group["body_mass_g"])
    print(f"{species}: n={len(group)}, correlation={correlation:.3f}")
```

## Visualize the relationship

Each point represents one penguin.
Colour distinguishes species.

```{python}
#| label: fig-flipper-mass
#| fig-cap: "Flipper length and body mass of penguins, coloured by species; observations with missing required values are excluded."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 5))

for species, group in clean.groupby("species"):
    ax.scatter(
        group["flipper_length_mm"],
        group["body_mass_g"],
        label=species,
        alpha=0.65
    )

ax.set_xlabel("Flipper length (mm)")
ax.set_ylabel("Body mass (g)")
ax.legend(title="Species")
ax.grid(alpha=0.2)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Interpretation

Among the 342 penguins with complete measurements, longer flippers
were associated with greater body mass.
The overall Pearson correlation was 0.871.
Within species, correlations were positive but smaller:
0.468 for Adelie, 0.642 for Chinstrap, and 0.703 for Gentoo.

The scatterplot shows Gentoo penguins generally clustered at longer
flipper lengths and greater body masses.
The stronger pooled correlation reflects both differences between
species and variation within species.
These observational results do not establish that longer flippers
cause greater body mass.
Two observations were excluded because of missing measurements.
